title: Review: Identification of ions by chemical and spectroscopic means (chemistry only); The composition and evolution of the Earth's atmosphere
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank for AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) (review status in the bank: authored-gated-unreviewed). Terms: 4.8.3-c02, 4.8.3-c11, 4.8.3-c04, 4.8.3-c06. Clues: 4.8.3-c02 first sentence of the bank's definition; 4.8.3-c11 first sentence of the bank's definition; 4.8.3-c04 first sentence of the bank's definition; 4.8.3-c06 first sentence of the bank's definition. Questions: 4.8.3-q11, 4.8.3-q23, 4.8.3-q27, 4.9.1-q21, 4.8.3-q12, 4.8.3-q28, 4.9.1-q22, 4.8.3-q13, 4.8.3-q30, 4.9.1-q23, 4.8.3-q14, 4.9.1-q24. The matching task revisits terms from the worlds it reviews, in a new mix.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Precipitate
items.clue: An insoluble solid formed when two solutions are mixed.

items.label: Yellow flame colour
items.clue: The flame colour produced by sodium compounds in a flame test.

items.label: Orange-red flame colour
items.clue: The flame colour produced by calcium compounds in a flame test.

questions.stem: Excess sodium hydroxide solution is now added to the three white precipitates formed from aluminium, calcium and magnesium ions. What happens?

options.text: Only the aluminium hydroxide dissolves.
Only the calcium hydroxide dissolves.
All three of the white hydroxides dissolve.
None of the three precipitates dissolves.

questions.explanation: Only the aluminium hydroxide precipitate dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide solution.

questions.stem: In Required practical 7 a student is given a solution of a single unknown ionic compound and must name it. Which plan will identify the compound?

options.text: adding sodium hydroxide, then more of it
adding barium chloride to test for chloride
just a flame test on its own is enough
a flame test, then a test for the anion

questions.explanation: The compound is named only when both its metal ion and its negative ion have been identified.

questions.stem: In flame emission spectroscopy the sample is put into a flame. What happens to the light given out, and what is the output?

options.text: It passes into a spectroscope, giving a line spectrum.
It is split by a coloured filter into one colour.
It passes through a coloured filter, giving one colour.
It warms a sensor, giving a temperature reading.

questions.explanation: The light given out is passed through a spectroscope and the output is a line spectrum.

questions.stem: Apart from photosynthesis, what else decreased the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere?

options.text: The burning of the fossil fuels that contain carbon in them
The release of nitrogen gas by the first plants and algae
The escape of carbon dioxide gas out into outer space
The formation of sedimentary rocks and fossil fuels holding carbon

questions.explanation: The specification states that carbon dioxide was also decreased by the formation of sedimentary rocks and fossil fuels that contain carbon.

questions.stem: Which set of metal ions all give coloured precipitates when sodium hydroxide solution is added to their solutions?

options.text: aluminium, calcium and magnesium ions
copper(II), iron(II) and iron(III)
copper(II), calcium and magnesium ions
aluminium, calcium and the iron(III) ion.

questions.explanation: Solutions of copper(II), iron(II) and iron(III) ions form coloured precipitates when sodium hydroxide solution is added.

questions.stem: A student is given the line spectrum of a solution together with a reference set of line spectra for known metal ions. The sample spectrum contains every line of the lithium reference and every line of the calcium reference. What should the student conclude?

options.text: Only the ion with the brighter lines is present.
Lithium ions and calcium ions are both present.
Only the ion with the most intense lines is present.
Nothing can be concluded from a spectrum like this.

questions.stem: Which sequence describes the main changes in the Earth's atmosphere over time?

options.text: Mainly oxygen at first, then carbon dioxide rising steadily to today
Mainly carbon dioxide, then oxygen rising as carbon dioxide fell
Mainly nitrogen at first, then volcanoes added the oxygen
Almost unchanged since the Earth formed 4.6 billion years ago

questions.explanation: The early atmosphere was mainly carbon dioxide; the oceans, photosynthesis and the formation of carbon-containing rocks and fuels lowered it while oxygen rose.

questions.stem: Sodium hydroxide solution is added to iron(III) chloride solution. What is seen?

options.text: a green precipitate forms
a blue precipitate forms
a white precipitate is formed
a brown precipitate is seen

questions.stem: A solution is analysed by flame emission spectroscopy. Sample lines (nm): 589, 671. Reference lines (nm): sodium 589; lithium 671; potassium 766; calcium 622. Which metal ions does the sample contain?

options.text: lithium and sodium ions
sodium ions on their own
sodium and potassium ions
potassium and calcium ions

questions.explanation: Both reference lines, 589 nm and 671 nm, appear in the sample.

questions.stem: How were deposits of limestone formed?

options.text: From thick layers of plant material buried in swamps
From plankton buried in mud and heated under pressure
From shells and skeletons deposited on the sea bed
From volcanic ash settling over the ocean floor

questions.explanation: Limestone is a sedimentary rock formed from the carbonate shells and skeletons of marine organisms, locking carbon out of the atmosphere.

questions.stem: A solution gives a green precipitate when sodium hydroxide solution is added. Which ion does the solution contain?

options.text: The solution contains iron(II) ions.
The solution contains copper(II) ions.
It is a solution of iron(III) ions.
It is a magnesium salt in water.

questions.stem: How did deposits of crude oil and natural gas form?

options.text: From plankton buried in mud on the sea bed
From trees and ferns buried in ancient swamps on land
From the shells of sea creatures on the sea bed
From volcanic gases trapped deep underground

questions.explanation: Crude oil and natural gas formed from the remains of plankton buried in mud and altered by heat and pressure over millions of years.
